desc:
Count how many structurally different binary search trees can store exactly the values 1, 2, ..., n, each value once. Two trees are different if their shapes differ (a node has a left child in one tree and not in the other, and so on).

Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

Example 1

n = 3
Output: 5
The root can be 1, 2 or 3. With root 2 there is exactly one tree; with root 1 or root 3 there are two trees each (2 + 1 + 2 = 5).

Example 2

n = 1
Output: 1
hints: Try n = 1, 2, 3, 4 by hand and look at the counts. Fix the root and see what is left to build.
If the root is the value i, the values smaller than i form the left subtree and the larger ones form the right subtree. The two subtrees are chosen independently.
Let f(k) be the answer for k values (f(0) = 1 for the empty tree). Then f(k) = sum over i of f(i) * f(k-1-i). Fill the table bottom-up modulo 1,000,000,007.
editorial: Let f(k) be the number of BSTs on k consecutive values. Only the number of values matters, not the values themselves. If the root is the (i+1)-th smallest value, the left subtree uses i values and the right subtree uses k-1-i values, and any left shape can be combined with any right shape, so f(k) = ∑i=0..k-1 f(i) · f(k-1-i) with f(0) = 1.

These are the Catalan numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ... A bottom-up loop takes O(n²) time and O(n) space. Products of two reduced values reach about 1018, so use a 64-bit type and reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 after each addition of a product (or after the whole sum if the sum is kept in a wide type). The closed form C(2n, n) / (n + 1) with a modular inverse gives O(n) as well.
